title: Why do we laugh when we're tickled?
subtitle: Knismesis and gargalesis
subject: sciences
description: A feather's brush is irritating; a hand under the armpits sets off helpless laughter. What skin, brain and play build together, and why you can't tickle yourself.
author: stacy-jankowski

hero.hook: Aristotle and Darwin racked their brains over it: why does a simple touch set off a laugh that nobody can control?

blocks.text: A hand creeps toward your ribs and off it goes: you squirm, you beg for it to stop, and yet you laugh. This small mystery has intrigued thinkers since antiquity. Socrates, Aristotle, then Francis Bacon, Galileo, René Descartes and **Charles Darwin** all took an interest in it.

Tickling looks like a trivial game. It is in fact a complex mechanism that combines the skin that feels, the body that reacts, emotion and several circuits in the brain. The result is **involuntary laughter**, a laugh you cannot command.

sections.title: Two kinds of tickle: knismesis and gargalesis

blocks.text: Researchers distinguish **two kinds** of tickling. The first is light, "like a feather": this is [[knismesis]]. It feels like an itch, can be felt almost anywhere on the body and does not make you laugh. An insect running along your arm: you shiver, but you do not burst out laughing.

blocks.caption: A fingertip brushing a child's back: knismesis, a light tickle that irritates more than it amuses.

blocks.text: The kind that triggers laughter is called [[gargalesis]]. It takes **quick and firm** movements, and it produces wriggling, writhing and laughter-like sounds that are impossible to hold back. The body processes it much like play. It only works on certain areas: armpits, neck, torso, stomach and feet.
To study gargalesis, researchers tickle **rats**: their vocalizations and their play behavior are well documented, which makes them a model of choice.

sections.title: From touch to laughter: the brain's circuit

blocks.text: It all starts in the skin. Touch is picked up there by [[mechanoreceptors]], sensory receptors that respond to pressure or movement. Their signal travels up to the brain and mixes there with the **signals of play**, emotional and behavioral: this blend switches on several circuits at once.

blocks.caption: A section of a human brain: the deep reward regions and the frontal cortex take part in the laughter circuit.

blocks.text: Deep regions linked to **reward** release [[dopamine]]: the tickle becomes a pleasant experience. To these are added the areas that process humor and emotions, and part of the [[salience network]], which sorts out what deserves our attention. Laughter itself starts somewhere else again: in the [[frontal operculum]] and the [[supplementary motor area]].

Despite all these circuits, there is no way to make yourself laugh by tickling your own feet. First explanation: **predictability**. When the brain knows in advance what the skin is about to feel, such as your own fingers sliding along the sole of your foot, it turns the signal down.

Second explanation: the other person is missing. Gargalesis is tied to play, and therefore to a **social situation**. When you tickle yourself, there is no partner and no exchange: the whole emotional and behavioral side of the response disappears. What is left is a touch on the skin, but no play, and so no laughter.

Nobody really knows why tickling appeared in the course of evolution. A first idea makes it a matter of **survival**: in mock fights, tickling teaches where the vulnerable areas of the body are, and we work out defense strategies that come in useful on the day of a real fight.

blocks.caption: A chimpanzee in Kibale Forest, Uganda: among our cousins too, play builds bonds.

blocks.text: The other idea is gentler: tickling would simply be a game, a behavior that brings people closer. Laughter shared between parents and children, between siblings, between friends, creates and maintains the **bond**. Combat training or social glue: the question remains open.
Tickle laughter comes from a firm tickle, gargalesis, which the skin, the reward circuits and the context of play turn together into involuntary laughter that cannot be reproduced on yourself.
